originalAction.text: Metformin’s established glucose-lowering action combines reduced glucose production by the liver, reduced intestinal glucose absorption and improved uptake and use of glucose by tissues. It improves insulin sensitivity without stimulating insulin secretion. Repurposing research asks whether changes in cellular energy sensing, growth signals and the handling of damaged cellular material can be useful beyond diabetes. AMPK is an energy-sensing enzyme, while mTOR signaling helps regulate protein production and cell growth; altering these systems can have different consequences in infected cells, tumors and healthy muscle. The evidence below distinguishes effects measured in experimental models from proposed explanations and from clinical outcomes, because demonstrating a pathway change does not establish that a treatment helps patients.

pathways.title: Insulin sensitivity and growth signaling
pathways.text: Improving insulin sensitivity is part of metformin’s established action in diabetes. In cancer repurposing, reducing insulin-related growth stimulation is one proposed route to benefit. The MA.32 breast-cancer trial measured changes in insulin, weight and other metabolic factors, but its clinical report did not show improved invasive disease-free survival. These findings distinguish a measured metabolic effect from an unconfirmed anticancer benefit.

pathways.title: AMPK, mTOR and the balance between energy use and growth
pathways.text: AMPK activation and reduced mTOR signaling provide a rationale for changing cell growth and protein production. In myeloma cell lines and mouse xenografts, metformin activated AMPK, suppressed mTORC1 and mTORC2 signaling, and was associated with autophagy, cell-cycle arrest and reduced tumor growth. In viral infection, suppression of host-cell protein production is a proposed explanation for reduced SARS-CoV-2 replication; the COVID-OUT nasal-swab study measured viral RNA rather than directly proving that mTOR mediated the reduction in viral RNA. The same growth-related pathways also matter in healthy tissue: mTORC1 supports muscle growth, and metformin reduced muscle gains during resistance training in the MASTERS trial. A mechanism that appears useful in one setting can therefore work against the intended outcome in another.

pathways.title: Autophagy and mitochondrial stress
pathways.text: Autophagy is the cell’s process for recycling cellular material. In Parkinson’s disease cell and mouse models, metformin was associated with AMPK activation and autophagy, less mitochondrial oxidative stress and reduced accumulation of alpha-synuclein. Blocking AMPK or autophagy weakened protection in toxin-injured cells, supporting a contribution from these pathways within that model. Inhibitor specificity, the experimental exposure and the difference between toxin injury and human disease limit translation; these experiments do not establish that metformin slows Parkinson’s disease in people.

pathways.title: Complex I inhibition and energy sensing
pathways.text: Two preclinical studies in cells and isolated mitochondria show that metformin inhibits complex I of the mitochondrial respiratory chain, the enzyme that initiates electron transfer during cellular respiration. In intact hepatoma cells, 50 micromolar metformin produced time-dependent inhibition of complex I activity, reducing glutamate oxidation by 13 percent after 24 hours and 30 percent after 60 hours; succinate oxidation, which enters at complex II, was unaffected, confirming selectivity for complex I. In a complementary study using isolated rat hepatocytes, inhibition of cell respiration by metformin occurred only in intact cells and not in permeabilized cells or isolated mitochondria, demonstrating that the mechanism requires an indirect, cell-mediated signaling step rather than direct drug contact with the enzyme. In isolated sub-mitochondrial particles, half-maximal inhibition required approximately 79 mM, far above therapeutic plasma concentrations, while the effect appeared at 50 micromolar in intact cells, consistent with intracellular drug accumulation. Reduced flux through complex I lowers cellular ATP production and is proposed to be one upstream trigger for the AMPK activation described in other pathway studies. These are preclinical findings from cell lines, isolated hepatocytes, and sub-cellular fractions; they do not establish the concentrations, tissue distribution, or extent of complex I inhibition during therapeutic metformin treatment in people.

pathways.title: Nitric oxide and guanylate cyclase in septic shock
pathways.text: The septic shock trial authors describe methylene blue as an inhibitor of inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) that also acts on its downstream enzyme, soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC). They state that, through indirect pressor effects, it has been shown to restore vasoregulation in conditions of nitric oxide upregulation, and they contrast it with non-selective nitric oxide synthase inhibition. The multicenter trial protocol adds that methylene blue blocks sGC, inhibits inducible nitric oxide synthase without affecting the constitutive enzyme, and converts nitric oxide to an inactive form, which lessens nitric oxide-mediated vasodilation. The single-center trial did not measure cytokine or nitrate/nitrite serum levels, so this mechanism was not directly confirmed in those patients.
